what: The control for Phasor Twin. Motor, gears, cranks, rods and both cylinder guides are the same, but the second crank plate is clocked to the same angle as the first instead of 90° ahead. Both pistons now move together. In the simulator both strokes stay 32.00 mm, while the loop that the two piston positions trace against each other collapses from 805.8 mm² to about 4 mm² per crank turn: a straight line.
try: Load this control, press Reset, then Run, and watch both piston rods: they now move side by side.
Compare with Phasor Twin: there one piston is at mid-stroke and moving fastest when the other stops at the end of its stroke.
Picture the two piston positions plotted against each other. In this control the points lie on a straight line; in Phasor Twin they go round a closed loop.
Check the strokes: both pistons still travel 32 mm, so only the phase has changed, not the motion of either piston alone.
why: The loop area ∮ x_A dx_B measures how far the two motions are out of step. For two crank-sliders with the same throw r it equals π r² sin φ, where φ is the phase between the throws. With φ = 0 the second piston always repeats the first, every step of one is matched by the same step of the other, and the enclosed area is zero. Nothing else in the machine changed, so the control shows that the area in Phasor Twin comes from the 90° clocking of the cranks.
matters: In a Stirling engine the two gas volumes must change out of step; an engine whose volumes move together encloses no area in its pressure–volume diagram and produces no net work, however fast it turns. The same check applies to any machine that needs a cycle: two motions in phase can be large, but they do not go round.
question: Both pistons still travel 32 mm. Why is the loop area almost zero in this control, while Phasor Twin encloses about 805 mm²?
answer: With the cranks clocked together the two pistons move in step, so their positions trace a straight line: the area π r² sin φ is zero for φ = 0. In Phasor Twin the cranks are 90° apart, sin φ = 1, and the area is π · (16 mm)² ≈ 804 mm².
further: Predict the loop area for a 45° clocking with π r² sin φ.
Which clocking gives the largest area, and why does 180° give zero again?
Why do Stirling engines use about 90° between the two volumes?
formula: A = ∮ x_A dx_B = π r² sin φ; φ = 0° here ⇒ A = 0 (simulator about 4 mm² per turn); Phasor Twin φ = 90° ⇒ A ≈ 804 mm².
